name: Pharmacogenomics
title: Pharmacogenomics
answer: Pharmacogenomics is the study of how inherited genetic variation changes a person's response to a drug, covering both how the body processes a medicine and how the medicine acts on its target. It sits inside genomic medicine and precision therapeutics, where the aim is to match a drug or a dose to a patient's genotype rather than to an average patient. The field draws on variants in genes such as CYP2D6, CYP2C19, TPMT and DPYD, and on the star allele nomenclature used to describe them. Its clinical reach spans psychiatry, oncology, cardiology and pain management, where dosing decisions are most often genotype sensitive.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Pharmacogenomics is the study of how inherited genetic variation changes a person's response to a drug, covering both how the body processes a medicine and how the medicine acts on its target. It sits inside genomic medicine and precision therapeutics, where the aim is to match a drug or a dose to a patient's genotype rather than to an average patient. The field draws on variants in genes such as CYP2D6, CYP2C19, TPMT and DPYD, and on the star allele nomenclature used to describe them. sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on genotyping platforms, from targeted panels and arrays through to whole exome and genome sequencing, plus the laboratory information systems that carry sample identity and results. Interpretation depends on curated knowledge bases that link variants to drug response, and on clinical decision support embedded in the electronic health record so that an alert reaches the prescriber at the moment of ordering. Reference laboratories, hospital pharmacies and informatics teams share this infrastructure, and the same variant may be reported through several different systems. Data standards for representing alleles and phenotypes are what allow those systems to agree with one another.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: A typical workflow starts with a sample, then genotyping or sequencing, then translation of raw variants into star alleles and a predicted metabolizer phenotype such as poor, intermediate, normal or rapid. That phenotype is paired with drug specific guidance, often drawn from published consensus recommendations, and returned to the clinician as an interpretive report. Machine learning enters mainly at the edges, for variant calling, for quality control, for phenotype prediction from sequence, and for flagging patients who may benefit from testing. Pharmacists and clinical geneticists frequently review the result before it is acted on, because the evidence base differs by gene and drug pair.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Pharmacogenomic testing raises questions about consent, return of results, and what happens to incidental findings that were never the reason for the test. Genetic information is treated as sensitive personal data in many jurisdictions, and rules on its handling vary widely, so laboratories and health systems maintain their own policies alongside statutory requirements. Provenance matters throughout: which assay was used, which reference sequence and knowledge base version was consulted, and when the interpretation was last updated. This site tracks 229 compliance and regulation pages, reflecting how much of the field's practical work now sits in documentation and audit rather than in the assay itself. Liability questions around clinical decision support remain unsettled, and this site follows 6 active product liability and wrongful death lawsuits against AI companies.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is toward preemptive testing, where a panel is run once and stored so that results are already available when a drug is later prescribed. That shift depends less on new science than on making results portable across institutions and readable by prescribing systems years after they were generated. Polygenic scores and pharmacogenomic risk are beginning to be combined, though the evidence for most such combinations is still thin. Wider sequencing will also surface variants of uncertain significance faster than guidance can be written for them, which keeps expert review in the loop. The field's near term constraint is likely to be implementation and reimbursement rather than discovery.
